newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British Steel pays price of firm pound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British Steel pays price of firm pound.

text.p: British Steel Plc counted the cost of the pound's relentless rise on world currency markets on Monday as its annual profits collapsed, forcing it to launch a cost-cutting drive which will cull more jobs and put the squeeze on suppliers.

Pretax profits were more than halved to 451 million pounds ($736.8 million) from 1.1 billion the previous year. The annual dividend was frozen at 10 pence per share and turnover was up a mere two percent at 7.22 billion pounds.
Sir Brian Moffat, chairman and chief executive, told a news conference that this year's job losses would exceed the 1,500 figure seen in the last financial year.
A provision of around 61 million pounds has been levied in the accounts published on Monday to pay for the 1997/98 job cuts, said a company spokesman.
The group's problems boiled down to two factors, said Moffat. "We had a double whammy of (steel) prices being too weak and the further impact of currencies."
British Steel's shares ended down 4-3/4 pence at 158-1/2 pence after the results, although the sharp fall in profits had been anticipated.
Terence Sinclair, analyst at Salomon Brothers, said the figures were "in line with what was expected, but the balance sheet was slightly stronger."
Moffat admitted in the results statement the year had been a "difficult" one, but made clear the pound's pain was not over despite brightening prospects in the steel market.
"The steel trading outlook for 1997/98 is one of cautious optimism, although concerns remain about the current strength of sterling and its serious impact on our future profits."
He issued a warning that the pain would be felt across Britain's export industry.

"The strength of sterling is a problem to British Steel and to many of its UK customers who are also significant exporters. Their order books are bound to be affected later this year if sterling remains at its present level," said Moffat.
As a result of the profit collapse, Moffat announced three price-cutting initiatives on Monday. The first is to speed up the job cutting programme.

He told the news conference that the speed of job losses hinged on how quickly British Steel could retrain its core staff to take on a wider range of duties. "We are still negotiating with unions on a plant-by-plant and year-by-year basis. We want to put everyone on the same working conditions," he said.
Recent press reports have speculated that the group could axe up to 10,000 jobs in five years, compared with the regular 500 to 1,000 jobs shed per annum.
A group spokesman told Reuters earlier this year the group would axe "significantly more than 5,000 jobs over five years" at a cost of tens of millions of pounds.
The other main target for cutting costs is British Steel's supplier base, which will also be squeezed hard.
Moffat made clear that a new more ruthless approach would be adopted. "We're trimming our supplier base. We want from our suppliers zero inflation, and cost benefits on top of that."
Moffat said British Steel wished to ask suppliers for the same exacting service it provided to its own major customers -- the automotive industry.
The third cost saving strategy is to improve information technology systems.

Salomon's Sinclair said be believed the total savings could be 700 million pounds per year, but added that the full benefit of those savings would not be felt until the cost-cutting drive was almost completed.

The root of British Steel's woes is the pound which has risen more than 20 percent against the mark since last summer leaving companies like British Steel exposed. Much of the group's mainland European sales is denominated in marks.
Some 80 percent of its sales are sterling-sensitive and some 55 percent of sales are non-domestic.
As well as being hit by sterling strength in mainland European markets, the company has also suffered cheaper competitors scooping up business in Britain.
British Steel's results also faced a separate blow of weak steel prices last year.
The net impact was average revenue per tonne sliding by eight percent, with the worst effects felt in the second half of the financial year.
Although British Steel has suffered from the pound's gains only in the last year, it has seen world steel prices declining since mid-1995 due to a slowdown in demand and destocking among customers.
But current trading conditions provided some signs of a comeback. Demand was described as "buoyant" in Britain, the U.S. and the Far East, with some improvement also seen in mainland Europe.
British Steel hopes the actions announced on Monday will stem the flow of lost profits as long as the pain inflicted by the pound does not get any worse.
When another analyst was asked what Moffat's likely response would be if the pound became even stronger, he replied, "Moffat would probably roll into a ball and weep." ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
